name: Schwarzwaldhaus

re.e: South-facing orientation with calibrated south windows maximises passive solar gain in winter; bioclimatic reviews confirm south-facing vernacular forms reduce heating demand by up to 40% in Cfb climates
Cattle quarters on ground floor act as radiant heat source; zoothermal gain from livestock estimated at 500–800 W per head, providing meaningful base-load heating in adjacent spaces
Dramatically overhanging eaves (1–1.5m) block high summer sun angle while admitting lower winter sun; a fundamental passive solar shading principle confirmed across vernacular temperate typologies
Steep roof pitch sheds snow load rapidly; prevents accumulation

cult: The Schwarzwaldhaus integrates farming life — livestock, hay, tools, and family — under one massive roof. This was a deliberate social-economic strategy of the Black Forest peasant economy: the entire farm could function self-sufficiently through winter without leaving the building. The roof was a symbol of pride and the farmer's wealth.
refs: Schütte, H. (1979). Das Schwarzwaldhaus. Württembergisches Landesmuseum.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.
Fernández-García, F. et al. (2024). A Review of Passive Solar Heating and Cooling Technologies Based on Bioclimatic and Vernacular Architecture. Energies, 17(5), 1006.
Moran, F. et al. (2014). Passive design in Southern European vernacular architecture. Energy and Buildings, 82, 91–99.

name: Fachwerkhaus

re.e: Wattle-and-daub or brick infill between oak frame provides thermal mass; Fraunhofer IBP measurements on comparable half-timbered walls record effective U-values of 0.8–1.2 W/m²K, with moisture buffering a critical secondary function
Larger windows on south facades; smaller north openings limit heat loss
Tight medieval street plans create mutual shading and reduce wind exposure; street-level wind speed reductions of 30–50% measured in comparable dense historic street networks

cult: The exposed timber frame was a visible social status marker — elaborate carved patterns indicated the owner's trade guild or wealth. The communal street pattern reflects medieval guild self-governance, where neighbours shared party walls and the economic life of the settlement was encoded in the building fabric.
refs: Binding, G. (1989). Fachwerkbau. Wissenschaftliche Buchgesellschaft.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.
Fraunhofer IBP (2020). Energy-efficient renovation of half-timbered buildings. Fraunhofer Institut für Bauphysik.
Haj Hussein, M. et al. (2021). Effect of thermal mass in heavyweight construction on indoor thermal environment. Journal of Physics: Conference Series, 2042, 012159.

name: Niederdeutsches Hallenhaus

re.e: Low gable end faces into prevailing wind; minimal exposed surface area
Deep thatch provides R-value ~3.0; moss-caulked joints ensure airtightness
Animals, threshing floor, and family share continuous hall for shared warmth

cult: The Niederdeutsches Hallenhaus was not merely a building type but the basic unit of North German agrarian political economy. The single roof sheltering animals, grain, tools, and family under one open hall dissolved the boundary between labour and dwelling — the threshing floor was worked in winter without leaving shelter. Farm names were legally heritable titles; the dugnad tradition of reciprocal construction labour meant the entire community was invested in each new building. The harsh maritime climate of the North Sea plain made this integration necessary: warmth was shared because it could not be individually produced.
refs: Bedal, K. (1993). Ländliche Hausbau in Deutschland. Stuttgart.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.
Fernández-García, F. et al. (2024). A Review of Passive Solar Heating and Cooling Technologies Based on Bioclimatic and Vernacular Architecture. Energies, 17(5), 1006.

name: Casa Patio / Cortijo

re.e: Central fountain combined with plants lowers courtyard air temperature by up to 12°C versus outdoor conditions in summer (Perez et al. 2023 Seville measurements), with 92% of daylight hours within thermal comfort range
High whitewashed walls shade ground during peak sun hours; wall reflectance ~0.8 and self-shading geometry provide mean radiant temperature reductions of 6–8°C at pedestrian level

60–80cm stone/adobe walls delay heat penetration 8–10 hours (thermal time constant ~8–12h); EnergyPlus models of comparable Mediterranean courtyard houses confirm near-zero mechanical cooling demand in summer when combined with night purging

cult: The patio tradition originates with the Roman atrium and was refined through eight centuries of Moorish rule in Al-Andalus. The enclosed garden is a cultural symbol of paradise (Arabic firdaws). The Córdoba Patios Festival (UNESCO Intangible Heritage) shows its ongoing function as a space of neighbourhood pride, display, and social identity.
refs: Rubio-Bellido, C. et al. (2015). Assessment of climate-responsive design in Cadiz. Building & Environment, 94, 507–516.
Perez, A. et al. (2023). Seasonal analysis of thermal comfort in Mediterranean social courtyards. Journal of Building Engineering, 78, 107611.
Domínguez-Torres, C. et al. (2021). Courtyard building configuration and performance: A systematic review. Energy and Buildings, 243, 110988.
Mehra, S.R. et al. (2025). Impact of courtyard microclimate on building thermal performance under hot weather conditions: A review. Energies, 18(20), 5433.
UNESCO (2024). Urban Heritage Atlas: Córdoba. World Heritage Centre. https://whc.unesco.org/en/urban-heritage-atlas/cordoba/
Alessandri, A. et al. (2014). Robust assessment of the expansion and retreat of Mediterranean climate in the 21st century. Scientific Reports, 4, 7211.

name: Trullo

re.e: Delays indoor heat gain and reduces daytime temperature peaks

re.s: Whitewashed exterior and conical roof geometry
re.e: Reduces absorbed shortwave radiation and limits overheated roof surfaces

re.s: Large stone mass around a small interior volume
re.e: Stabilizes indoor temperature by shifting heat release toward evening and night

re.s: Corbelled stone roof without timber structure
re.e: Creates a roof span from abundant limestone rather than scarce wood

re.s: Sloped stone roof and underground storage
re.e: Turns episodic rainfall into stored domestic water supply

cult: The trullo is a dry-stone dwelling typology from the limestone plateau of Puglia, where hot summers, strong solar exposure, limited timber, and seasonal water scarcity shaped a compact mineral architecture. Thick limestone walls and conical stone roofs create high thermal inertia, slowing daytime heat gain and releasing stored heat after sunset. Whitewashed surfaces reduce absorbed solar radiation, while small openings and compact interior volume limit unwanted heat exchange. Its climatic logic depends on mass, reflectance, geometry, and locally abundant stone rather than mechanical cooling.
refs: Laviano, R. et al. (2010). I trulli di Alberobello. Politecnico di Bari.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.

Cardinale, N. et al. (2013). Energy and microclimatic performance of Mediterranean vernacular buildings: The Sassi district of Matera and the Trulli district of Alberobello. Building and Environment, 59, 590–598.
Rospi, G. et al. (2016). Energy and Environmental Performance of Trullo Stone Building. International Journal of Heat and Technology, 34(S2), S229–S235.
Alessandri, A. et al. (2014). Robust assessment of the expansion and retreat of Mediterranean climate in the 21st century. Scientific Reports, 4, 7211.
lesson: The trullo is not simply a cool stone house. Its performance depends on the combined presence of thermal mass, reflective limewash, compact geometry, limited openings, rainwater capture, and enough night cooling to discharge stored heat.

name: Sassi di Matera

re.e: Ground temperature and stone mass dampen summer heat and winter cold

re.s: Semi-buried dwellings with limited exposed roof and wall area
re.e: Minimizes solar gain on occupied surfaces compared with freestanding buildings

re.s: Hewn cisterns, channels, and porous stone catchments
re.e: Captures episodic rainfall and stores it within the settlement fabric

re.s: Courtyards, openings, and drainage paths require continuous maintenance
re.e: Shows the limit of the strategy: mass and ground contact must be paired with air and water management

cult: The Sassi di Matera are a rock-cut settlement system carved into soft tuff, where dwellings, cisterns, paths, and courtyards work as one ground-coupled infrastructure. Rather than treating the cave as a primitive shelter, the system uses geological mass to buffer extreme seasonal variation, shields most occupied surfaces from direct solar radiation, and stores scarce rainwater in excavated cisterns. Its climatic intelligence lies in coupling habitation, water management, and topography.
refs: Laureano, P. (1993). Giardini di pietra. Bollati Boringhieri.
UNESCO World Heritage Documentation (1993).
Cardinale, N. et al. (2009). Energy and microclimatic performance of restored hypogeous buildings in south Italy: The 'Sassi' district of Matera. Building and Environment, 44(5), 1046–1054.

Cardinale, N. et al. (2013). Energy and microclimatic performance of Mediterranean vernacular buildings: The Sassi district of Matera and the Trulli district of Alberobello. Building and Environment, 59, 590–598.
Alessandri, A. et al. (2014). Robust assessment of the expansion and retreat of Mediterranean climate in the 21st century. Scientific Reports, 4, 7211.
lesson: The transferable lesson is not to copy cave dwelling as form, but to use ground coupling, thermal lag, protected openings, and water storage as an integrated environmental system. Without ventilation, sanitation, and moisture control, earth-embedded strategies can also produce serious health risks.

name: Wind Catcher Houses (Badgir)

re.e: Badgir tower funnels prevailing wind downward: Hosseini et al. (2016) CFD simulations of six Yazd wind-catcher geometries show indoor air velocities of 0.5–1.5 m/s under 3 m/s external wind; Hedayat et al. (2017) long-term field measurement confirms cooling effectiveness even when wind speed peaks

Air passes over qanat underground water channel (12–14°C) before entering rooms; combined wind-tower and qanat system achieves indoor temperature reductions of up to 15°C below ambient — Nejat et al. (2021) estimate cooling load reduction of 73% versus a reference building in hot season
All rooms face inward; zero glazing on hot street-facing facades

cult: The badgir is Persian urban civilization materialized. The qanat — underground water channels — was collective civic infrastructure. Wind tower height signalled the owner's wealth. Yazd's entire city was engineered as a passive climate machine.
refs: Bahadori, M.N. (1978). Passive cooling systems in Iranian architecture. Scientific American, 238(2), 144–154.
Hosseini, G. et al. (2016). Evaluation of airflow and thermal comfort in buildings ventilated with wind catchers in Yazd City, Iran. Energy for Sustainable Development, 35, 7–24.
Hedayat, Z. et al. (2017). Wind energy and natural ventilation potential of a wind catcher in Yazd, Iran: A long-term measurement. International Journal of Green Energy, 14(8), 650–655.
Nejat, P. et al. (2021). Passive cooling and natural ventilation by the windcatcher (Badgir): An experimental and simulation study. Journal of Building Engineering, 41, 102436.
Ahmadikia, H. et al. (2012). Performance analysis of a wind-catcher with water spray. International Journal of Green Energy, 9(7), 689–703.
Fathy, H. (1986). Natural Energy and Vernacular Architecture. United Nations University Press.
Foruzanmehr, A. (2012). Summer-time thermal comfort in vernacular earth dwellings in Yazd, Iran. Archnet-IJAR, 6(3), 60–75.

name: Adobe Pueblo

re.e: 50–80cm adobe walls absorb solar heat by day and release it through the cold desert night; Balcomb et al. (1983) Southwest Thermal Mass Study at Tesuque Pueblo measured buildings supplying 18–78% of annual heating need passively depending on glazing ratio and orientation
Buildings step back at each storey creating shaded outdoor terraces

South-facing mass maximises winter solar gain; combined with high desert insolation (~300 days/year) adobe construction achieves positive heat balance without supplementary heating for significant portions of the heating season

cult: Pueblo architecture is inseparable from Ancestral Puebloan cosmology — room layout, kivas, and plazas reflect astronomical alignments and ritual calendars. Multi-storey form with no individual ground-floor entrances reflects egalitarian social structure. Taos Pueblo is a UNESCO World Heritage living site.
refs: Knowles, R.L. (1974). Energy and Form. MIT Press.
Balcomb, J.D. et al. (1983). Southwest Thermal Mass Study, Tesuque Pueblo, New Mexico. DOE/SF/11493. U.S. Department of Energy.
Shukla, A., Tiwari, G.N. & Sodha, M.S. (2009). Thermal performance of an adobe structure integrated with an earth-air heat exchanger. International Journal of Energy Research, 33, 1059–1069.
Fathy, H. (1986). Natural Energy and Vernacular Architecture. United Nations University Press.

name: Ghadamès Old Town

re.e: Date palm canopy reduces ambient temperature by 5–8°C
Houses connected at upper storey create fully shaded ground-level streets
Buildings form continuous wind barrier; tiny ventilation holes only

cult: Ghadamès has a unique gendered spatial structure: upper-storey covered streets were traditionally reserved for women, while men used ground-level paths. This division is directly encoded in the architecture. A major trans-Saharan trade hub — its covered passageways were commercial and climatic infrastructure simultaneously.
refs: UNESCO (2001). Ghadamès World Heritage Documentation.
Vellinga, M. et al. (2007). Atlas of Vernacular Architecture of the World. Routledge.
Osman, M.M. & Serageldin, M. (1981). Ghadames: A model of human settlements in Sahara. Habitat International, 5(5–6), 695–713.
Fathy, H. (1986). Natural Energy and Vernacular Architecture. United Nations University Press.

name: Rumah Panggung (Stilt Houses)

re.e: 1–3m stilts create continuous airflow beneath floor: Feriadi & Wong (2004) field survey of 525 Indonesian naturally ventilated houses confirms significantly higher adaptive comfort satisfaction than PMV predicts, with under-floor ventilation a primary driver of moisture management and perceived comfort
2–3m overhangs protect walls; 50–60° roof pitch sheds monsoon rain rapidly — deep eaves measured to reduce wall exposure to driving rain by over 80% in comparable tropical vernacular houses
Floor raised above flood level; water passes beneath harmlessly

cult: The Borneo longhouse was a political structure — entire community lived under one roof, each family with its own hearth. Longhouse length signified the chief's power. The communal veranda (ruai) hosted ceremonies, dispute resolution, and daily work. The building was literally the community's social constitution.
refs: Waterson, R. (1990). The Living House: An Anthropology of Architecture in South-East Asia. Thames & Hudson.
Feriadi, H. & Wong, N.H. (2004). Thermal comfort for naturally ventilated houses in Indonesia. Energy and Buildings, 36(7), 614–626.
Bassaleng, D. et al. (2024). Thermal performance of vernacular stilt house in Palu City. Civil Engineering and Architecture, 12(3), 1523–1531.
Biwole, P.H., Woloszyn, M. & Pompeo, C. (2008). Heat transfers in a double-skin roof ventilated by natural convection in summer time. Energy and Buildings, 40(8), 1417–1428.

name: Mekong Delta Vernacular

re.e: Shaded verandas on multiple sides shade rooms and capture cross-breezes; Nguyen et al. (2011) field investigation of Vietnamese vernacular housing identifies veranda depth and multi-directional orientation as the most decisive passive cooling strategies in humid tropical Vietnam

Ventilated ridge allows convective hot air to escape upward; stack-effect ventilation in comparable tropical ridge-vented roofs reduces indoor operative temperature by 2–4°C relative to sealed roof constructions
Elevated platform separates structure from saturated tropical ground

cult: The Mekong Delta house stood in an intimate, ambiguous relationship with water: the river was road, food source, and seasonal threat simultaneously. Structures were deliberately lightweight and modular — lashed bamboo and timber construction could be disassembled and moved as land ownership, flooding, and family circumstance changed. The veranda-as-dock collapsed the distinction between domestic threshold and waterway, making social life continuous with the movement of commerce. Climate adaptation here was not insulation or mass but adaptability: the right to relocate was itself a climate strategy.
refs: Dili, A.S. et al. (2011). Passive control measures for building comfort in Vietnam. Energy Conversion and Management, 52(10), 3392–3399.
Feriadi, H. & Wong, N.H. (2004). Thermal comfort for naturally ventilated houses in Indonesia. Energy and Buildings, 36(7), 614–626.
Nguyen, A.T. et al. (2011). An investigation on climate-responsive design strategies of vernacular housing in Vietnam. Building and Environment, 46(10), 2088–2106.

name: Kerala Nalukettu

re.e: Central open nadumuttam draws hot air upward; cool air drawn in through shaded verandas
45° gable + massive overhangs drain rain and protect walls
Jali lattice allows ventilation while blocking direct solar penetration

cult: The Nalukettu is a cosmological diagram — the nadumuttam aligns with cardinal directions and sacred geometry. Room sequence encodes Nair caste social hierarchy. The house is simultaneously a climate machine and a ritual space for births, marriages, and funerals.
refs: Tripathi, A. et al. (2025). Analyzing climate-responsive vernacular architecture in Kerala. OEIL Research Journal.
Chandel, S.S. et al. (2016). Review of energy efficient features in vernacular architecture for improving indoor thermal comfort. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 65, 459–477.
Sharma, T. (2006). Traditional responses of moisture related decay mitigation in timber architecture of Travancore (Kerala). Dist.Unina.It.
Tipnis, A. (2012). Vernacular Traditions: Contemporary Architecture. TERI Press.

name: Tongkonan

re.e: Boat-shaped saddle roof with overhangs of 1.5–2m sheds monsoon rain rapidly while shading walls; the curved form reduces wind pressure on the ridge compared to a gabled profile, improving structural performance in typhoon conditions

Bamboo absorbs excess humidity and releases it when air dries — hygroscopic buffering capacity ~10% of dry weight measurably dampens indoor RH peaks during monsoon periods relative to timber-framed equivalents
Elevated floor on stilts creates continuous under-floor air circulation

cult: The tongkonan is both climate machine and political instrument. Its construction demands collective labour, ritual sacrifice of buffalo, and the physical participation of all clan members — the act of building reaffirms social hierarchy and spiritual obligation simultaneously. The boat-shaped roof, oriented north-south, is understood as the vessel carrying ancestors. Material choices are ecological signals: bamboo for moisture regulation, ironwood for structural permanence, palm thatch graded by social rank. The raised floor creates the ventilated undercroft that makes tropical habitation tolerable — but it is also the space where livestock and ritual objects are kept. Thermal function and cosmological meaning are inseparable.
refs: Waterson, R. (1990). The Living House: An Anthropology of Architecture in South-East Asia. Thames & Hudson.
Feriadi, H. & Wong, N.H. (2004). Thermal comfort for naturally ventilated houses in Indonesia. Energy and Buildings, 36(7), 614–626.
Biwole, P.H., Woloszyn, M. & Pompeo, C. (2008). Heat transfers in a double-skin roof ventilated by natural convection in summer time. Energy and Buildings, 40(8), 1417–1428.

name: Icelandic Turf House (Torfbær)

re.e: 1m+ turf walls and roof achieve substantial insulation: Hansen et al. (2008) building physics analysis confirms turf walls functioned as thermally insulating envelopes, with wall geometry and material arrangement derived empirically to optimise thermal comfort in a climate with minimal building material alternatives

Low profile and semi-buried footprint reduce wind loading and exploit stable ground temperature (~4°C): Hansen et al. note farmhouse siting on natural or man-made elevations was strategic — combining shelter from wind with drainage and thermal stability
Long entrance tunnel acts as airlock preventing warm air escaping

cult: Extreme material scarcity — no building timber in Iceland. Norse settlers improvised entirely from the landscape: turf, volcanic stone, and driftwood. The farmstead cluster was a subsistence economy in architectural form. In use until the mid-20th century.
refs: Sigurðardóttir, Þ. (2010). Turf Houses in Iceland. Minjasafn Austurlands.
Hansen, T.K. et al. (2008). The historical turf farms of Iceland: Architecture, building technology and the indoor environment. Building and Environment, 43(6), 1038–1046.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.

name: Sami Goahti

re.e: Conical form minimises heat-loss surface area relative to enclosed volume; at the goahti's typical diameter of 3–4m, the geometry reduces envelope heat loss by approximately 20–30% compared to a rectangular room of equal floor area
Multiple reindeer-hide layers added in winter, removed in summer: hide thermal conductivity ~0.04 W/mK; three layers achieve R-value ~1.5 m²K/W — meaningful insulation in −30°C subarctic conditions
Frame disassembles in minutes; entire dwelling carried by reindeer sledge

Goahti is sited in natural topographic hollows or against rock outcrops; windward snow accumulation around the structure provides additional insulation — average 30–50% reduction in convective heat loss compared to exposed flat-ground siting

cult: The goahti is the material form of Sami sovereignty over landscape. Its portability was not a limitation but a political capacity: the ability to follow reindeer herds across seasonal territories was the economic and cultural foundation of Sami life. The interior geography — hearth at centre, altar-back at the far wall, gender-coded entry sides — encodes the social order of the family in spatial form. The conical birch-pole frame and layered hide covering were calibrated over centuries to the specific thermal demands of subarctic nomadic life: maximum insulation per unit of carried weight, rapid erection and dismantling, and a single central opening that serves simultaneously as smoke exit, light source, and sky compass.
refs: Nordin, J.M. (2002). Sami Architecture in Northern Scandinavia.
Vellinga, M. et al. (2007). Atlas of Vernacular Architecture of the World. Routledge.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.

name: Mongolian Ger

re.e: Circular plan distributes wind loads evenly — no corners to catch wind

Multiple felt layers added in winter, removed in summer: Li et al. (2019) field measurement confirms felt thermal conductivity ≤0.077 W/mK (equivalent to expanded polystyrene), but notes the ger's low thermal inertia produces large diurnal indoor swings — the adjustable layering system compensates for what single-layer construction cannot

Crown toono acts as chimney flue in winter and opens fully for stack-effect ventilation in summer; Ganbat et al. (2020) experimental comparison shows gers with enhanced envelope insulation achieve indoor operative temperatures up to 5°C higher during cold nights than uninsulated reference gers

cult: The ger is a cosmological diagram: the toono represents the sky eye; the central post is the world axis. North is sacred/elder space, west is male/livestock, east is female/domestic. The ger's portability enabled the Mongol Empire to govern a continent from moveable capital cities. Contemporary research identifies the ger's coal combustion for heating as a major driver of Ulaanbaatar's severe winter air pollution — the adaptive performance that sustained nomadic life creates critical health challenges in its fixed urban context.
refs: Goldstein, M.C. & Beall, C.M. (1994). Nomads of Western Tibet. University of California Press.
Ganbat, D. et al. (2020). Experimental investigation and energy performance simulation of Mongolian Ger with ETS heater and solar PV in Ulaanbaatar City. Energies, 13(21), 5840.
Li, Y. et al. (2019). Experimental study on the indoor thermo-hygrometric conditions of the Mongolian yurt. Sustainability, 11(3), 687.
Enkhbat, E. & Kistelegdi, I. (2019). Comparative analysis for traditional yurts using thermal dynamic simulations in Mongolian climate. Energy Procedia, 158, 3523–3528.

name: Dogon Cliff Settlement

re.e: Bandiagara escarpment provides permanent shade from scorching afternoon sun
Surrounding sandstone acts as massive thermal sink
Thick laterite-painted adobe walls resist hot dry wind penetration

Thick laterite-adobe walls (40–60cm) maintain interior temperature within ±3°C of overnight minimum even as outdoor temperature climbs 25–30°C during the day — the escarpment's thermal mass amplified at building scale

cult: The Dogon settled the near-vertical face of the Bandiagara escarpment as a survival decision: the cliff was a defense against the waves of slave raiding that devastated the West African interior from the 14th to 19th centuries. The thermal logic arrived as a consequence — the escarpment's sandstone mass absorbs and moderates the brutal Sahel heat, and the cliff overhangs shade the settlement through the hottest afternoon hours. Village plans encode the Dogon creation myth: each settlement maps onto a lying human figure oriented east-west, with granaries as limbs and the toguna meeting house as head. The Tellem cliff caves above the living settlements are maintained as ancestral burial sites, making the escarpment simultaneously a dwelling, a cosmological diagram, and a cemetery.
refs: Lane, P. (1996). The Dogon revisited. World Archaeology, 28(2), 193–219.
Vellinga, M. et al. (2007). Atlas of Vernacular Architecture of the World. Routledge.

name: Djenné Adobe Town

re.e: Mud walls 40–60cm thick absorb daytime heat and radiate it outward at night; banco (mud-straw composite) has thermal conductivity ~0.5 W/mK and high volumetric heat capacity — the wall acts as a phase-shift buffer, keeping interiors cool by day and preventing rapid overnight heat loss
Protruding timber torons are permanent scaffolding for annual community re-plastering
Residents sleep on roof terraces when walls radiate stored heat at night

cult: The Great Mosque's annual re-plastering is a community ritual — hundreds of citizens climb the toron scaffolding together on a single day. A festival of social solidarity as much as maintenance. The city's survival is inseparable from this annual collective act of climate-responsive repair.
refs: Maas, P. & Mommersteeg, G. (1992). Djenné. ORSTOM.
UNESCO (1988). Old Towns of Djenné World Heritage Documentation.
Rael, R. (2009). Earth Architecture. Princeton Architectural Press.
Minke, G. (2006). Building with Earth: Design and Technology of a Sustainable Architecture. Birkhäuser.

name: Moroccan Riad

re.e: Central fountain lowers courtyard temperature by 3–6°C via evaporation; combined with vegetation, Perez et al. (2023) measurements in comparable Andalusian courtyard typologies show courtyards up to 12°C cooler than outdoor ambient in peak summer and up to 3.3°C warmer at night
Street-facing facades have zero glazing; all rooms open exclusively inward
Deliberate asymmetry prevents sun reaching courtyard floor at any angle

cult: The riad embodies the Quranic concept of paradise — the garden as foretaste of heaven. The blank street wall reflects Islamic domestic privacy: the house is a world turned entirely inward, its beauty reserved for the family alone. Social status expressed through interior refinement, invisible from the street.
refs: Fathy, H. (1973). Architecture for the Poor. University of Chicago Press.
Perez, A. et al. (2023). Seasonal analysis of thermal comfort in Mediterranean social courtyards. Journal of Building Engineering, 78, 107611.
AlAnzi, A. et al. (2009). Impact of courtyard geometry on the thermal performance of buildings in hot dry climates. Building and Environment, 44(1), 138–144.
Hillenbrand, R. (1994). Islamic Architecture: Form, Function and Meaning. Columbia University Press.
Bianca, S. (1999). Hofhaus und Paradiesgarten: Architektur und Lebensformen in der islamischen Welt. Prestel.

name: Ahmedabad Pol Houses

re.e: Narrow pol lanes remain in shade for most of the day

Carved timber jali lattice allows ventilation while blocking direct sun; Jain & Pandya (2022) show traditional sandstone jalis with 30–50% void ratio transmit only 30–45% of incident solar radiation, with air velocity through perforations measured at 0.5–1.0 m/s under natural wind conditions
Shared walls distribute thermal mass load across the entire cluster

cult: The pol is a complete neighbourhood unit — gated cluster with shared temple, well, and waste management. Each pol housed a single caste or trade community. Facade carvings were markers of craft identity: patterns varied by caste, making the street a readable social text. The pol system was urban self-governance predating the modern municipality.
refs: Desai, M. et al. (2012). The Pol Houses of Ahmedabad. CRUTA Foundation.
Jain, K.K. & Pandya, D.V. (2022). Significance of Jaali on thermal performance of buildings. Materials Today: Proceedings, 57, 2181–2187.
Chandel, S.S. et al. (2016). Review of energy efficient features in vernacular architecture for improving indoor thermal comfort. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 65, 459–477.

name: Andean Stone Houses

re.e: Stone masonry absorbs powerful daytime highland sun (solar irradiance at 3,500–4,000m is 15–20% higher than sea level due to reduced atmospheric attenuation); volcanic andesite thermal diffusivity ~0.7 mm²/s releases stored heat with a 6–8 hour lag, warming interiors through the coldest overnight hours

Ichu grass (Stipa ichu) thatch provides thermal resistance of ~0.3–0.5 m²K/W per 10cm depth; at typical roof thicknesses of 30–50cm, total R-value ~1.0–2.5 m²K/W, meaningful where nighttime temperatures fall 20°C below daytime peaks
Building clusters face east to warm quickly after the coldest pre-dawn hours

Agricultural terraces (andenes) are engineered to drain cold air downslope on still nights, keeping the inhabited plateau edge 2–4°C warmer than the valley floor — frost protection encoded in landscape form

cult: Andean stone construction embeds climate knowledge accumulated across three thousand years of high-altitude settlement. The Inca did not invent the thermal logic of the pirca — dry-stone masonry walls used as solar collector by day, radiator by night — but systematised it as imperial infrastructure. The terraced landscape (andenes) was simultaneously agricultural engineering, microclimate modification, and flood control: cold air drainage down terraced slopes was a designed condition. Stone selection was thermal as much as structural — dark volcanic andesite on south-facing walls for maximum solar absorption, pale granite on north-facing faces to limit heat loss. East-facing cluster orientation to capture the first light after the coldest pre-dawn hours is a bioclimatic strategy encoded in Andean settlement patterns long before any formalised climate science.
refs: Gasparini, G. & Margolies, L. (1980). Inca Architecture. Indiana University Press.
Vellinga, M. et al. (2007). Atlas of Vernacular Architecture of the World. Routledge.

name: Cappadocian Cave Dwellings

re.e: Volcanic tuff maintains stable 12–15°C year-round, regardless of outdoor extremes
Zero external surface area to solar gain; entire structure buried in rock
Small windows only; rock insulates from wind and prevents convective heat loss

cult: Cappadocia's caves span Hittite, early Christian, and Ottoman contexts. Underground cities descending 18 stories were built for communal defense. The tuff landscape became a canvas for religious expression: thousands of cave churches survive at Göreme. Material is both architecture and geology.
refs: Rodley, L. (1985). Cave Monasteries of Byzantine Cappadocia. Cambridge University Press.
Cardinale, N. et al. (2013). Energy and microclimatic performance of Mediterranean vernacular buildings. Building and Environment, 59, 590–598.
Alessandri, A. et al. (2014). Robust assessment of the expansion and retreat of Mediterranean climate in the 21st century. Scientific Reports, 4, 7211.

name: Norwegian Laftehus Farmstead

re.e: Round logs with saddle notches and moss-caulked joints achieve low air infiltration; comparable Norwegian log construction measured at 0.5–1.5 ACH50 in field tests — approaching passive house standards through traditional craft alone

Living turf roof absorbs rainfall and releases it via evapotranspiration; comparable Scandinavian sod roofs reduce peak runoff by 60–80% versus impermeable roofing, while evapotranspiration provides measurable cooling of the roof surface in summer
Outbuildings arranged as protective U-shape shelter main dwelling

Norwegian farmsteads orient the main residential facade south or south-east; combined with the U-shaped outbuilding windbreak, this creates a protected sun-trap courtyard that measurably extends outdoor habitation season

cult: The Norwegian gård was a legal entity before it was an architectural one: the farm name (gårdsnavnet) was the heritable title defining family identity across generations, and the buildings were evidence of that claim. Laftehus log construction required dugnad — reciprocal community labour that built and maintained rural settlements across Scandinavia. The stabbur, a raised log storehouse mounted on stone pillars to deter rodents and moisture, is the most climate-precise element: its elevated, ventilated position maintains the cool stable temperature needed for long-term food storage through both summer and winter, encoding a passive refrigeration logic that the main dwelling could not provide.
refs: Stoklund, B. (1980). Building Traditions in the Northern World. Copenhagen.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.
Hansen, T.K. et al. (2008). The historical turf farms of Iceland: Architecture, building technology and the indoor environment. Building and Environment, 43(6), 1038–1046.

name: Musgum Earthen Shells

re.e: Thick clay catenary walls keep interior 8–10°C cooler than outside through thermal mass; the catenary form (identical to a hanging-chain curve) distributes compressive loads optimally, allowing walls to taper from thick at base to thin at apex — structurally efficient and thermally responsive simultaneously
Raised external ribs channel rainwater to ground rapidly without pooling

Small hole at apex creates stack effect drawing hot air upward and out; the high internal volume under the dome allows warm air to stratify above the occupied zone — the principle is identical to a thermal chimney

cult: The Musgum developed the catenary shell — mathematically identical to a hanging chain — without formal geometry. The ribs were interpreted by Western architects as aesthetic, but are structural buttresses. A case study in vernacular structural intuition: optimal engineering form through generations of material practice.
refs: Vellinga, M. et al. (2007). Atlas of Vernacular Architecture of the World. Routledge.
Rael, R. (2009). Earth Architecture. Princeton Architectural Press.
Minke, G. (2006). Building with Earth: Design and Technology of a Sustainable Architecture. Birkhäuser.

name: Fujian Tulou
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: 1.5–2m thick rammed earth wall delays heat transfer 10–12 hours; Li et al. (2012) field energy survey of Nanjing Tulou buildings confirms better indoor thermal environment than surrounding non-mass construction, with thick walls and large summer ventilation rates identified as primary performance drivers
All openings face courtyard and sky; air continuously flushed through structure
Steep roof sheds monsoon rain; central courtyard manages runoff via drainage system
Perimeter corridor and wide overhangs shade the inward timber facade

cult: The tulou was a fortified clan compound housing 700–800 people of a single surname for mutual defense against bandits and territorial raids. The circular form provides equal defensive sightlines. The central courtyard contains communal wells, ancestral halls, and granaries. UNESCO World Heritage site and symbol of Hakka ethnic identity.
refs: Huben, H. & Guillaud, H. (2022). Earth Construction. China Academy of Art Press.
Li, Q. et al. (2012). Characterizing the household energy consumption in heritage Nanjing Tulou buildings, China. Energy and Buildings, 49, 317–326.
Sun, X. et al. (2014). Measurement and simulation of thermal environment in heritage Nanjing Tulou buildings. In: Proceedings of ICIEA 2014, Springer.
Wang, Q. (2000). Vernacular Dwellings. Ancient Chinese Architecture. Springer.

name: Nalukettu
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Central open nadumuttam draws hot air upward; cool air in through shaded verandas
Steep tiled gable + massive overhangs drain rain rapidly; protect walls
Lattice allows ventilation while blocking direct solar penetration
Courtyard pond and dense shrubs lower perceived temperature via evapotranspiration

cult: The Nalukettu is a cosmological diagram — the nadumuttam aligns with cardinal directions and sacred geometry. Room sequence (public veranda → semi-public hall → private rooms) encodes Nair caste social hierarchy. The house is simultaneously a climate machine and a ritual space.
refs: Tripathi, A. et al. (2025). Analyzing climate-responsive vernacular architecture in Kerala. OEIL Research Journal.
Chandel, S.S. et al. (2016). Review of energy efficient features in vernacular architecture for improving indoor thermal comfort. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 65, 459–477.
Feriadi, H. & Wong, N.H. (2004). Thermal comfort for naturally ventilated houses in Indonesia. Energy and Buildings, 36(7), 614–626.
Sharma, T. (2006). Traditional responses of moisture related decay mitigation in timber architecture of Travancore (Kerala). Dist.Unina.It.
Tipnis, A. (2012). Vernacular Traditions: Contemporary Architecture. TERI Press.

name: Impluvium Hut
typology: Circular earth hut with compluvium roof
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Two-layer thatch (1.7m eave / 6.75m ridge) creates deep shade with ventilated air gap
Compluvium channels rain into central basin — water storage and microclimate modifier
Earth walls absorb heat; moisture absorption regulates interior humidity
Multiple entrances from different directions enable cross-ventilation

cult: The circular compound is the basic spatial unit of Casamance social organisation — each hut houses one family member; the shared courtyard is communal kitchen and social space. The compound grows with the family: new huts added as children marry. The dwelling is literally grown by the family it houses.
refs: Kane, M.N. et al. (2023). Construction techniques in vernacular earth building in humid tropical climate. Journal of Building and Construction Planning Research, 11, 1–18.
Minke, G. (2006). Building with Earth: Design and Technology of a Sustainable Architecture. Birkhäuser.

name: Traditional Thai House
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Floor elevated above maximum flood level; water passes beneath harmlessly

Gaps between clustered houses and parallel windows enable full cross-ventilation: Tantasavasdi et al. (2001) show optimal ventilation requires window openings of 40–60% of wall area and inter-building gaps of at least 0.5× building width to avoid wind shadow effects
2–3m high concave gable with extra eave sheds rain from all angles
Ground acts as thermal buffer below the elevated floor

cult: The Thai house cluster is structured around kinship — each module added as a child marries. The open terrace between houses is the social heart: eating, sleeping, and ceremonies. Houses orient toward the river/canal, reflecting the centrality of water in lowland Thai agricultural culture.
refs: Tantasavasdi, C. et al. (2001). Natural ventilation design for houses in Thailand. Energy and Buildings, 33(8), 815–824.
Kubota, T. et al. (2009). Effects of control parameters on wind-driven cross ventilation in residential buildings. Building and Environment, 44(9), 1817–1825.
Biwole, P.H., Woloszyn, M. & Pompeo, C. (2008). Heat transfers in a double-skin roof ventilated by natural convection in summer time. Energy and Buildings, 40(8), 1417–1428.

name: Shophouse
typology: Colonial urban terrace with air well
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Internal narrow air well (typically 0.9–1.5m wide) creates strong stack effect: 3–5°C temperature differential between ground and roof drives upward air movement of 0.3–0.8 m/s — sufficient for perceptible comfort improvement without mechanical assistance
Mandatory arcade buffers facade from direct sun and monsoon rain
Adjustable louvres calibrate ventilation and privacy independently

cult: The shophouse is a hybrid of colonial encounter — Chinese domestic courtyard type adapted to British street regulations (five-foot way mandate). In Penang, facade styles record waves of migration: Hokkien, Peranakan, Art Deco, British. George Town's shophouse streetscape is UNESCO-listed.
refs: Zwain, A. & Bahauddin, A. (2017). Traditional courtyard components of shophouses in Penang. Planning Malaysia Journal, 15(1).
Bay, J-H. & Ong, B.L. (eds) (2006). Tropical Sustainable Architecture: Social and Environmental Dimensions. Architectural Press.
Cheah, A.J. et al. (n.d.). Ventilation system and comfort level of a traditional shophouse in Kuala Lumpur. Universiti Teknologi Malaysia.

name: 33rd Lane (Geoffrey Bawa)
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: No rooms face the hot street; all face inward courtyards as lightwell and ventilation chimney — Perera & Pernice (2022) measure outdoor transitional spaces in Sri Lankan modernist houses reducing indoor operative temperatures by 2–3°C versus direct-exposure rooms in comparable tropical urban conditions
Completely glassless — open timber lattice windows allow maximum airflow year-round
Multiple shade layers (overhang, veranda, pergola, plants) block direct sun

cult: Bawa's 33rd Lane is a manifesto for tropical modernism — deliberately rejecting air conditioning and embracing traditional Sri Lankan spatial strategies within a modern language. The house evolved over decades as Bawa connected four adjacent properties — a palimpsest of accumulation rather than a designed object.
refs: Robson, D. (2002). Geoffrey Bawa: The Complete Works. Thames & Hudson.
Rajapaksha, I. et al. (2003). Natural ventilation in courtyard buildings: Multi-storey living in the tropics. Architectural Science Review, 46(3), 295–303.
Jazeel, T. (2017). Tropical modernism/environmental nationalism: The politics of built space in postcolonial Sri Lanka. Fabrications, 27(2), 134–152.

Perera, D. & Pernice, R. (2022). Modernism in Sri Lanka: A comparative study of outdoor transitional spaces in selected traditional and modernist houses. Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering, 22(3), 1013–1028.

name: Ena de Silva House
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Every room ventilated from at least two sides via distributed courtyard network
Verandas, overhangs, pergolas, and dense plants prevent direct solar reach to any wall
Large pool provides evaporative cooling and bounces diffuse light into rooms

cult: Designed for batik artist Ena de Silva, the house dissolves the boundary between inside and outside. Later controversially disassembled and rebuilt at a new location, raising fundamental questions about what constitutes the essence of architecture. A manifesto and a provocation simultaneously.
refs: Robson, D. (2002). Geoffrey Bawa: The Complete Works. Thames & Hudson.
Rajapaksha, I. et al. (2003). Natural ventilation in courtyard buildings: Multi-storey living in the tropics. Architectural Science Review, 46(3), 295–303.
Jazeel, T. (2017). Tropical modernism/environmental nationalism: The politics of built space in postcolonial Sri Lanka. Fabrications, 27(2), 134–152.
Nunes, I.L. (2023). Women architects disrupting tropical modernism. Traditional Dwellings and Settlements Review, 34(2), 7–22.
Perera, D. & Pernice, R. (2022). Modernism in Sri Lanka: A comparative study of outdoor transitional spaces. Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering, 22(3), 1013–1028.

name: Bedok Court
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Each unit has a 4.5×4.5m private forecourt providing outdoor space and ventilation
East-west massing captures prevailing wind; semi-open facade allows through-ventilation
Stacked forecourts and gallery overhangs shade the floor below

cult: Bedok Court challenged the assumption that public housing must be anonymous towers. The private forecourt became a site of personalisation: residents planted their own gardens. At 300 persons/hectare it proved courtyard principles achievable at high density.
refs: Bay, J-H. (2004). Sustainable community in tropical Singapore high-rise housing. Architectural Research Quarterly, 8(3–4), 333–342.
Wong, N.H. & Chen, Y. (2010). Tropical Urban Heat Islands: Climate, Buildings and Greenery. Taylor & Francis.

name: Space Block
studio: TUM Chair of Building Technology & Climate Responsive Design
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Clustered layout with 50% void creates continuous wind channels through the block
Long axis E-W to face prevailing south-east breezes at up to 5.5 m/s
Narrow external slits block direct sun; full-height interior openings maximise ventilation

cult: The Space Block translated the Vietnamese tube house's air-well logic to collective scale. The 50% porosity principle came from studying traditional shophouses. Criticisms of concrete heating, lack of vegetation, and maintenance now directly feed the next generation of tropical dense housing design.
refs: Ebner, P. et al. (2010). Typology +: Innovative Residential Architecture. Birkhäuser.
Nguyen, A.T. et al. (2011). An investigation on climate-responsive design strategies of vernacular housing in Vietnam. Building and Environment, 46(10), 2088–2106.

name: Kepenek
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Creates a shaded, wind-buffered microclimate around the body
Traps still air and reduces convective heat loss during rest

re.s: Garment doubles as clothing and temporary enclosure
re.e: Provides protection without separate building infrastructure

re.s: Felt surface resists wetting and dries in air
re.e: Maintains protection under intermittent exposure

cult: The kepenek is a wearable felt shelter used by shepherds in Turkish and Kurdish pastoral landscapes. It sits between garment, portable architecture, and emergency refuge: thick felt buffers wind, cold, rain, and solar exposure, while its stiff form can stand around the body during rest. Its value is operational mobility—the shelter travels with the occupant rather than waiting at a fixed site.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Olgay, V. (1963). Design with Climate: Bioclimatic Approach to Architectural Regionalism. Princeton University Press.
lesson: The kepenek shows that climate adaptation can be body-scale infrastructure. Its transferability lies in portable insulation and shade, not in copying a pastoral object outside its livelihood context.

name: Khasi Knup
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Directs rain away from body and carried loads

re.s: Back-mounted form rather than hand-held umbrella
re.e: Allows work to continue during rain and sun
Reduces direct radiation on head, neck, and upper back
Creates repairable climate protection from local materials

cult: The Khasi knup is a body-scale shelter from the monsoon landscapes of Meghalaya. Its broad, curved form covers the head, back, and carried loads while leaving the hands free for agricultural work. Made from bamboo and leaves, it is a lightweight climatic interface that converts rainfall and solar exposure into a manageable occupational condition.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Chandel, S.S. et al. (2016). Review of energy efficient features in vernacular architecture for improving indoor thermal comfort. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 65, 459–477.
lesson: The knup belongs in the atlas because it shows climate adaptation as work infrastructure: shelter is scaled to movement, posture, labour, and rain intensity.

name: Black Hair Tent
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.s: Loose goat-hair weave and open sides
re.e: Provides shade while allowing convective heat removal
Tightens the weave and improves water shedding
Allows settlement to follow seasonal grazing and water availability

re.s: Fabric sides adjusted by wind direction
re.e: Balances ventilation with protection from wind-driven exposure

cult: The black hair tent is a mobile textile architecture adapted to arid and semi-arid pastoral life. Goat hair behaves dynamically: in dry heat the woven fabric remains breathable, while under rain the fibres swell and tighten, improving water resistance. The tent therefore performs through material responsiveness, low thermal mass, ventilation, shade, and rapid assembly rather than permanence.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Ecevit, N.C. (2007). Black tent architecture: A case study on climatic design principles. METU Journal of the Faculty of Architecture, 24(2), 1–18.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.
lesson: Its key transferable idea is adaptive porosity: a membrane can change its environmental behaviour with humidity, tension, layering, and operation.

name: Mashrabiya
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Reduces direct sun on glass, wall surfaces, and occupants near the façade
Breaks high-contrast sunlight into softer interior illumination
Allows air exchange while reducing exposure and maintaining privacy

re.s: One-way visual filtering from interior to street
re.e: Supports adaptive use of openings in dense urban fabric

cult: The mashrabiya is a dense climatic and social interface rather than a simple decorative screen. Its projecting wooden lattice shades the opening, breaks down glare, permits air movement, and preserves privacy. Because it modulates radiation, view, airflow, and social boundary at once, it is a strong example of a strategy family where environmental and cultural performance are inseparable.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Castritius, N. et al. (2026). The Sixth Facade. SHIFT Courtyard Edition, TUM.
Bagasi, A.A. et al. (2024). Novel integration of Mashrabiya and heat-transfer devices for passive cooling. Journal of Building Engineering, 82, 108211.
Beheiry, S. et al. (2025). Energy consumption analysis of using Mashrabiya as a retrofit solution. Buildings, 15(14), 2532.
Hillenbrand, R. (1994). Islamic Architecture: Form, Function and Meaning. Columbia University Press.
Abdelkader, R. & Park, J.-H. (2018). Sustainable building façades: Modern usages of the traditional Mashrabiya. Open House International, 43(2).
lesson: The transferable lesson is the calibrated porous boundary: opening size, depth, material, privacy, maintenance, and local wind conditions matter more than the ornamental pattern alone.

name: Jali Screen
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Self-shading apertures reduce direct solar penetration
Softens daylight and reduces contrast inside

re.s: Permeable screen at window or courtyard edge
re.e: Maintains airflow while reducing radiant exposure
Allows occupants to use openings without full visual exposure

cult: Jali screens use carved stone perforations to transform intense sun into filtered light and ventilation. Their depth and aperture geometry create self-shading edges, reduce glare, and maintain privacy while allowing air to pass. As a stone screen, the jali also adds thermal mass at the opening rather than relying on lightweight shading alone.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Jain, K.K. & Pandya, D.V. (2022). Significance of Jaali on thermal performance of buildings. Materials Today: Proceedings, 57, 2181–2187.
Kabre, C. (2022). Jaali: A tool of sustainable architectural practice. Ain Shams Engineering Journal, 13(3), 101613.
lesson: A jali is not any perforated panel. Its performance depends on aperture ratio, depth, orientation, material conductivity, and whether air movement is actually available.

name: Shōji Screen
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Washi paper scatters direct light into soft diffuse interior illumination with transmittance ~90%; Inoue et al. (2014) heat insulation tests show taiko-shoji (double-layer shoji with air gap) significantly reduces heat loss in winter compared to single-layer, validating the Japanese practice of seasonal double-layering
The screen maintains enclosure while preserving daylight and perceptual connection
Rooms can be opened, closed, or reconfigured according to time, use, and weather

cult: Shōji are not insulation — Japanese architecture accepts cold and negotiates with it rather than excluding it. The screen calibrates atmosphere: light quality, privacy depth, room definition, and airflow resistance are all adjusted by sliding and stacking panels. Washi paper's transmittance close to 90% while completely diffusing direct sunlight produces the soft interior illumination that is a defining quality of Japanese domestic space — diffused light without glare makes tatami rooms usable through the full arc of the day. The modular bay system (ken) underlying shōji dimensioning is simultaneously a structural grid, a spatial planning module, and a furniture standard: three systems unified by one measure.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Izard, J-L. & Ait-Ameur, K. (2007). Thermal comfort in the traditional Japanese house. In: PLEA 2007 Proceedings, Singapore.

Inoue, T. et al. (2014). Evaluation of heat insulation performance of the fitting combined taiko-shoji and wooden pair glass sash. Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering, 13(1), 97–104.

name: Capiz Shell Window
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Thin shell panes (1–2mm Placuna placenta) diffuse daylight with ~40–60% visible light transmittance while partially blocking infrared; measured interior illuminance in capiz-screened rooms of 150–400 lux under tropical overcast sky — adequate for domestic tasks without glare
Large panels can be adjusted for rain protection and ventilation
The shell membrane admits light but blurs direct views into domestic interiors

cult: The capiz shell window is an artefact of the Philippine colonial encounter: a pre-Hispanic technique of using thinly-sliced Placuna placenta shells as translucent infill, adopted and systematised in the bahay na bato (stone house) that emerged from Spanish colonial urbanism in the 17th–19th centuries. The shell's wavelength-selective transmittance — passing visible light while partially attenuating infrared — was discovered empirically centuries before it could be explained optically. The shells are harvested from shallow coastal beds, polished and sliced to 1–2mm, and set in wooden grid frames: a craft requiring specialised knowledge of both marine ecology and woodworking, concentrated in specific coastal communities.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Oliver, P. (1997). Encyclopaedia of Vernacular Architecture. Cambridge University Press.

name: Engawa
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: The overhanging roof edge and raised timber strip shade the room perimeter: Izard & Ait-Ameur (2007) thermal comfort measurements in traditional Japanese houses find the engawa reduces solar radiation by ~70 W/m² at the perimeter — meaningful protection that also functions as a buffer zone against rain and cold infiltration
Engawa separates interior rooms from rain-exposed garden edges
Screens and sliding doors allow the threshold to shift between interior, semi-outdoor, and outdoor use

cult: The engawa is a climatic and social threshold: neither fully inside nor outside. It mediates garden, room, light, rain, and everyday sitting practices.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Izard, J-L. & Ait-Ameur, K. (2007). Thermal comfort in the traditional Japanese house. In: PLEA 2007 Proceedings, Singapore.

Inoue, T. et al. (2014). Evaluation of heat insulation performance of the fitting combined taiko-shoji and wooden pair glass sash. Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering, 13(1), 97–104.

name: Thinnai
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: The platform sits under the roof edge creating a cooler resting zone; shaded threshold spaces in Tamil Nadu show mean radiant temperature 8–12°C lower than adjacent unshaded street surfaces during midday, with wind speed slightly elevated by the Venturi effect between building and overhang
Daily activities shift to a shaded edge where airflow and social exchange are maintained
The threshold protects entry and visitors during rain while keeping the dwelling permeable

The thinnai makes shade a shared public resource: the overhang covers not only the occupant but the visitor and passerby, embedding a logic of thermal commons into domestic architecture at the street edge

cult: The thinnai is a social-climatic interface in Tamil houses: a shaded platform for resting, receiving visitors, and occupying the street edge without full exposure.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Chandel, S.S. et al. (2016). Review of energy efficient features in vernacular architecture for improving indoor thermal comfort. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 65, 459–477.

name: Bologna Porticoes
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Porticoes shade pedestrian routes and reduce radiant exposure at street level; Antonini et al. (2020) people-flow study in Bologna city centre confirms direct correlation between portico shade and pedestrian dwell-time, and Possega et al. (2026) WRF climate simulations show Bologna's UHI intensity worsening under future high-emission scenarios — foregrounding the portico's structural relevance beyond heritage
The arcade maintains walkability and public life during wet weather
A continuous shaded circulation system extends domestic thresholds into the public realm

cult: Bologna's porticoes form a city-scale threshold system. They are legally, socially, and climatically embedded: private buildings produce a continuous public environmental infrastructure. Recent WRF climate modelling (Possega et al. 2026) shows Bologna's UHI strengthening under high-emission scenarios, with extreme thermal discomfort days nearly doubling over the last decade — making the portico's historical cooling function newly urgent for climate adaptation.
refs: Günther, M. & Schmidt, J. (2025). World Wide Vernacular Shading Tools. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2021). The Porticoes of Bologna.
Antonini, E. et al. (2020). The relation between outdoor microclimate and people flow in historic city context: The case study of Bologna within the ROCK Project. Energies, 13(18), 4766.
Possega, M. et al. (2026). Analysis of urban thermal structures in different scenarios of hot weather: The Bologna case study. Urban Climate, 55, 101957.

name: Lhasa Storey Building
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Courtyard and gallery oriented south-facing capture winter solar radiation: at Lhasa's latitude (29.7°N), a south-facing masonry gallery receives ~4,500–5,000 Wh/m²/day on clear winter days — among the highest passive solar resource densities on earth due to altitude-enhanced irradiance
Gallery limits summer overheating while admitting lower winter sun
Stone walls absorb daytime solar heat and release it slowly after sunset

cult: The Lhasa storey house navigates an extreme thermal range: winter temperatures reach −16°C while high-altitude summer solar radiation can heat south-facing stone surfaces above 50°C. A seasonal logic of occupation mediates this: winter draws life inward and down, into sun-trap courtyards and south-facing galleries; summer drives it up, onto flat roof terraces for sleeping, cooking, and drying. The white lime plaster exterior reflects summer radiation and is renewed annually at Losar (Tibetan New Year), maintaining albedo. Larsen & Sinding-Larsen's Lhasa Atlas (2001) documents how the repetition of this house type across the old city creates a coherent urban thermal environment: the aggregate of individual solar strategies becomes a collective microclimate.
refs: Schlosser, D. (2026). Learning from Vernacular: Cold / Highlands. SHIFT Courtyard Edition, TUM.
Vellinga, M. et al. (2007). Atlas of Vernacular Architecture of the World. Routledge.
Herrle, P. & Wozniak, A. (2023). Tibetan Houses: Vernacular Architecture of the Himalayas and Environs. Birkhäuser.
Alexander, A. (2013). The Traditional Lhasa House: Typology of an Endangered Species. LIT Verlag.
Larsen, K. & Sinding-Larsen, A. (2001). The Lhasa Atlas: Traditional Tibetan Architecture and Townscape. Shambhala.

name: Henan Troglodyte Courtyard
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.e: Excavated loess walls provide self-shading and earth-coupled thermal mass; earth-coupled construction of this type stabilises indoor temperature within a narrow band comparable to the Sassi di Matera and Cappadocian cave typologies — Cardinale et al. (2013) measurements across Mediterranean cave dwellings show seasonal indoor temperature maintained at 12–18°C year-round without mechanical systems
Surrounding earth buffers external temperature swings and reduces wind exposure
The courtyard floor is shielded from prevailing wind by surrounding ground mass

cult: The Henan yaodong courtyard is produced by excavation rather than construction. It converts the ground into wall, roof, thermal buffer, and wind protection, making the courtyard an inhabitable void within the loess plateau.
refs: Schlosser, D. (2026). Learning from Vernacular: Cold / Highlands. SHIFT Courtyard Edition, TUM.
Perez, A. et al. (2023). Seasonal analysis of thermal comfort in Mediterranean social courtyards. Journal of Building Engineering, 78, 107611.
Wang, Q. (2000). Vernacular Dwellings. Ancient Chinese Architecture. Springer.
Sun, F. (2013). Chinese climate and vernacular dwellings. Buildings, 3(1), 143–172.

name: Antakya Courtyard House
instructors: Bilge Kobas, Prof. Thomas Auer, Martin Despang

re.s: Narrow courtyard with shaded walls and galleries
re.e: Reduces radiant exposure while maintaining outdoor habitability
Delays heat transmission and stabilizes indoor temperatures

re.s: Openings toward courtyard and upper air escape
re.e: Promotes air exchange without full street exposure

re.s: Occupants shift between shaded courtyard, rooms, and terraces
re.e: Uses behavioural adaptation as part of the climatic system

cult: The Antakya courtyard house is a hot-summer Mediterranean dwelling organized around shaded interior openness. The courtyard is not an empty void; it is a thermal and social regulator that admits air and light while buffering the street. Masonry mass, vegetation, water, shaded galleries, and seasonal room use combine to shift daily life toward the coolest zones of the house.
refs: Frizzi, V., Nuzzi, F., Shimizu, K. & Pérez, À. (2026). COURTivate. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
Journal of Architecture and Planning (2024). Antakyan courtyard house documentation.
Perez, A. et al. (2023). Seasonal analysis of thermal comfort in Mediterranean social courtyards. Journal of Building Engineering, 78, 107611.
Vellinga, M. et al. (2007). Atlas of Vernacular Architecture of the World. Routledge.
Alessandri, A. et al. (2014). Robust assessment of the expansion and retreat of Mediterranean climate in the 21st century. Scientific Reports, 4, 7211.
lesson: The courtyard works as an inhabited microclimate only when combined with shade, mass, ventilation paths, and seasonal occupation patterns.

name: Pingyao Long Courtyard
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer · Martin Despang

re.s: South-oriented rooms and elongated courtyard geometry
re.e: Improves winter solar access and reduces exposed façade area

re.s: Narrow proportions and inward roof edges
re.e: Limits direct solar exposure on walls and courtyard surfaces

re.s: High perimeter walls and inward openings
re.e: Reduces convective heat loss and dust intrusion

re.s: Rooms arranged by orientation and family hierarchy
re.e: Allows seasonal migration within the house according to comfort

cult: The Pingyao long courtyard uses elongated inward space to manage a continental climate with cold winters, hot summers, wind, and solar exposure. The linear courtyard organizes family life while controlling orientation, enclosure, and seasonal sunlight. Roofs, walls, and courtyard proportions create protected outdoor space and allow rooms to benefit from winter sun while reducing summer exposure.
refs: Schlosser, D. (2026). Learning from Vernacular: Cold / Highlands. SHIFT Courtyard Edition, TUM.
lesson: Its logic is seasonal calibration: the same courtyard must collect, block, and distribute solar energy differently across the year.

name: Chentsa Wind-Protected Farming House
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer · Martin Despang

re.e: Reduces wind speed and protects household/agricultural activity
Stores daytime solar heat and reduces thermal fluctuation

cult: A highland farming courtyard where rammed-earth enclosure converts an exposed windy site into a protected domestic and productive microclimate.
refs: Schlosser, D. (2026). Learning from Vernacular: Cold / Highlands. SHIFT Courtyard Edition, TUM.

name: Hotan Pergola Courtyard
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer · Martin Despang

re.e: Reduces direct radiation on courtyard floor and walls
Improves perceived coolness through shade and plant transpiration

re.s: Leaves shade in summer, bare structure admits winter sun
re.e: Provides seasonal solar control without mechanical adjustment
Creates a social and climatic refuge from exposed streets

cult: The Hotan pergola courtyard responds to arid continental heat by turning vegetation and shade into an architectural layer. Grapevines and light structures shade the courtyard during the hot season while allowing seasonal change. The strategy creates a habitable intermediate climate between exposed desert air and enclosed rooms.
refs: Schlosser, D. (2026). Learning from Vernacular: Cold / Highlands. SHIFT Courtyard Edition, TUM.
lesson: Vegetated shading is climate infrastructure: it depends on irrigation, seasonal growth, maintenance, and the availability of dry air for evaporative benefit.

name: Córdoba Patio
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer · Martin Despang

re.s: Tall surrounding walls, arcades, and planting
re.e: Reduces direct solar exposure on occupants and surfaces

re.s: Potted plants, fountains, and moist surfaces
re.e: Adds localized evaporative cooling and humidity moderation
Creates a protected microclimate inside dense urban fabric

re.s: Watering, plant care, and seasonal canopy use
re.e: Turns architecture and daily maintenance into one adaptive system

cult: The Córdoba patio is a dense urban courtyard strategy for hot, dry Mediterranean summers. It compresses outdoor space into a shaded, vegetated, often watered interior room. Plants, porous surfaces, water vessels, shade, and high surrounding walls lower radiant exposure and create a cooler social core within the building.
refs: Frizzi, V., Nuzzi, F., Shimizu, K. & Pérez, À. (2026). COURTivate. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
lesson: Its performance depends on shade depth, vegetation health, water availability, and ventilation. Without these, a patio can become a heat trap rather than a cool refuge.

name: Casablanca Riad Courtyard
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer · Martin Despang

re.s: Tall perimeter walls and shaded galleries
re.e: Protects rooms and occupants from direct solar exposure

re.s: Planting and water at the centre
re.e: Adds localized cooling and improves perceived freshness

re.s: Blank exterior and active interior garden
re.e: Allows openings and outdoor life without street exposure

re.s: Open courtyard coupled with surrounding rooms
re.e: Enables heat release and air movement when outdoor conditions allow

cult: The riad courtyard mediates hot sun, privacy, and urban density through inward orientation. Its central garden and water elements create a shaded, evaporative core, while surrounding rooms are protected from the street and organized around cooler interior air. The strategy works through enclosure, vegetation, water, and controlled openings rather than exposed façades.
refs: Frizzi, V., Nuzzi, F., Shimizu, K. & Pérez, À. (2026). COURTivate. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
lesson: The riad is transferable as a courtyard microclimate principle, but not as a sealed inward type without ventilation, water management, and social compatibility.

name: Madonie Masseria
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer · Martin Despang

re.e: Delays heat transfer and stabilizes adjacent spaces

re.s: Courtyard links storage, dwelling, livestock and work
re.e: Supports work and social life while moderating exposure

cult: The masseria frames adaptation through rural productivity: the courtyard is a work yard, storage organiser, social space, and thermal buffer.
refs: Frizzi, V., Nuzzi, F., Shimizu, K. & Pérez, À. (2026). COURTivate. SHIFT Studio, TUM.

name: Polish Ogącanie
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer

re.s: Temporary straw or reed insulation on exposed façades
re.e: Reduces conductive heat loss during the heating season

re.s: Organic layer removed after winter and reused agriculturally
re.e: Links thermal adaptation to seasonal resource cycles

cult: Ogącanie reframes insulation as a seasonal practice rather than a fixed product: low-tech, reversible, and tied to agricultural material cycles.
refs: Boeck, M., Ladrouz, E., Lipcsei, B., Tanghe, E. & Taschner, J. (2025). Material as Thermal Regulation. SHIFT Studio, TUM.

name: Dammuso
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Damps daytime heat gain and stabilizes indoor temperature

re.s: Small openings and robust masonry envelope
re.e: Limits infiltration, dust, and wind-driven heat exchange
Reduces solar absorption and lowers roof-surface overheating

re.s: Domed roof channels rainfall into cisterns
re.e: Converts rare rainfall into a reliable domestic reserve

cult: The dammuso of Pantelleria translates an exposed volcanic island climate into a compact stone dwelling. Thick lava-stone walls buffer heat, wind, and salt-laden air; domed white roofs reflect radiation and guide rainwater toward cisterns; and small openings reduce solar and wind exposure. The type works as an environmental storage device: it stores coolness, stores water, and reduces exchange with a hot, dry, windy exterior.
refs: Boeck, M., Ladrouz, E., Lipcsei, B., Tanghe, E. & Taschner, J. (2025). Material as Thermal Regulation. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
lesson: Its transferability depends on diurnal cooling, massive local masonry, careful water collection, and low internal gains. In humid climates, mass without ventilation may become a liability.

name: Santorini Whitewashed Townhouse
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Reduces absorbed shortwave radiation and surface temperature
Delays heat transfer into occupied spaces

re.s: Narrow stepped lanes and compact building spacing
re.e: Cuts direct solar exposure in movement spaces

re.s: Mineral surfaces, compact volumes, and limited openings
re.e: Maintains habitable interiors with minimal active infrastructure

cult: Santorini’s whitewashed houses and cave-like rooms combine reflectance, mass, compactness, and settlement morphology. The white lime finish reduces solar absorption; thick volcanic masonry and excavated interiors moderate heat; and narrow shaded passages reduce pedestrian exposure. The climatic performance is therefore not only the colour white, but the coupling of surface albedo with mass, shade, and dense urban form.
refs: Boeck, M., Ladrouz, E., Lipcsei, B., Tanghe, E. & Taschner, J. (2025). Material as Thermal Regulation. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
lesson: Whitewashing is most effective when combined with low window-to-wall ratios, shaded outdoor circulation, and high-mass construction. Applied alone to lightweight buildings, it is only a surface treatment.

name: Cairo Salsabil Courtyard Cooling
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer

re.s: Water film over carved salsabil slab
re.e: Cools incoming air through phase change and increases perceived freshness

re.s: Water device placed in shaded interior or courtyard zone
re.e: Prevents direct solar heating of water and occupants

re.s: Stone/masonry surfaces around cooled air path
re.e: Adds thermal inertia to the evaporative cooling effect
Avoids overclaiming performance in humid climates where evaporation potential is low

cult: The salsabil is a water-and-air device embedded in courtyard architecture. A thin film of water flows over a carved or inclined surface, increasing the contact area between water and air. In a shaded courtyard or reception room, this supports evaporative cooling while the surrounding mass and enclosure moderate radiant heat. Its performance is strongest in hot-dry conditions and weakens as humidity rises.
refs: Boeck, M., Ladrouz, E., Lipcsei, B., Tanghe, E. & Taschner, J. (2025). Material as Thermal Regulation. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
lesson: The transferable principle is not decorative water, but controlled air–water contact in shaded, low-humidity air. It requires water availability, maintenance, and ventilation paths.

name: Cartuja Qanat
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer

re.e: Limits evaporation and protects water from solar heating

re.s: Water travels below the overheated surface layer
re.e: Maintains cooler water temperatures and reduces loss
Provides water movement with minimal operational energy
Creates secondary evaporative and shaded microclimates

cult: The qanat is not a building form but an infrastructural climate strategy: underground water conveyance uses gravity, soil insulation, and evaporation control to move water across arid landscapes. In architectural terms, it extends the thermal logic of the building into the ground, where water is protected from solar radiation and high evaporative loss.
refs: Bovier, L., Febi, R., Jamesieon, G. & Ohlenmacher, J. (2025). Ventilation and Porosity. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
lesson: The transferable logic is subsurface distribution and protection of water, not the literal replication of historic qanat construction everywhere.

name: Dolat Abad Windcatcher
instructors: Bilge Kobas · Prof. Thomas Auer

re.s: Tall shaft captures higher wind velocities
re.e: Draws air into interior spaces with lower direct solar exposure

re.s: Air passes near pools or moist surfaces
re.e: Reduces air temperature where evaporation potential is high

re.s: Thick masonry rooms connected to air path
re.e: Combines air movement with thermal lag
Avoids uncontrolled exposure while preserving cooling potential

cult: The Dolat Abad windcatcher links air movement, height, pressure difference, and water-cooled interior space. Its tall tower captures higher, faster air streams and directs them downward through shaded masonry volumes. Coupled with pools and thick walls, the system turns wind into a controlled cooling resource rather than relying on exposed openings at street level.
refs: Bovier, L., Febi, R., Jamesieon, G. & Ohlenmacher, J. (2025). Ventilation and Porosity. SHIFT Studio, TUM.
lesson: Windcatchers are transferable only where wind direction, dust, humidity, and maintenance are addressed. The tower is part of a coupled air path, not an isolated symbolic element.
